name: Makonde carving
subtitle: The Makonde live on a plateau divided by the Rovuma River between Tanzania and Mozambique.

facts.label: Where
facts.value: Makonde people live on a plateau on both sides of the Rovuma River, in Tanzania and Mozambique, and the two groups differ socially, in culture and language.

facts.label: Masks
facts.value: Makonde mapiko masks are worn during an initiation dance ritual, where each dancer represents a spirit.

facts.label: Who carves and wears
facts.value: A member of the men's secret society carves the mask and another member wears it and dances during a ceremony for new initiates.

facts.label: How a mask is made
facts.value: A mask in the Ditsong collection is of light wood, probably nyala, with strips of black beeswax added to the face to accentuate scarification.

facts.label: Colonial market
facts.value: The colonial market for Makonde carvings developed in the 1930s as Portugal consolidated control over northern Mozambique.

facts.label: What was carved for sale
facts.value: Local artists adopted ivory and ebony and carved small ethnographic busts, tropical animals and chess sets for their European patrons.

facts.label: Change in status of carving
facts.value: Before blackwood carving became popular, Mozambican Makonde artists mainly produced wooden masks for mapiko masquerade performances.

facts.label: Cooperatives
facts.value: Constantino Mpakulo, a Mozambican Makonde carver in Dar es Salaam in the 1950s and 1960s, helped create the Manamba sculptural cooperative.

facts.label: Everyday objects
facts.value: Makonde in Mozambique and Tanzania used ebony for utilitarian items such as combs, lip plugs and snuff containers.

parts.text: The Makonde live on a plateau divided by the Rovuma River between Tanzania and Mozambique. Their carvers made masks for mapiko initiation dances; in the colonial era Mozambican Makonde artists also developed blackwood carving for sale, and carvers working in Dar es Salaam formed cooperatives in the 1950s and 1960s.
